entries.0e9bf783e72289fed1e7d6754d885721c218a57f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv116"/><title type="x-ms">Ephesians</title> <div sID="gen31797" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31798" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Some</hi> think that this epistle to the Ephesians was a circular letter sent to several churches, and that the copy directed to the Ephesians happened to be taken into the canon, and so it came to bear that particular inscription. And they have been induced the rather to think this because it is the only one of all Paul's epistles that has nothing in it peculiarly adapted to the state or case of that particular church; but it has much of common concernment to all Christians, and especially to all who, having been Gentiles in times past, were converted to Christianity. But then it may be observed, on the other hand, that the epistle is expressly inscribed (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">1.1</reference>) <hi type="italic">to the saints which are at Ephesus;</hi> and in the close of it he tells them that he had sent Tychicus unto them, whom, in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2 Tim. iv. 12</reference>, he says he had sent to Ephesus. It is an epistle that bears date out of a prison: and some have observed that what this apostle wrote when he was a prisoner had the greatest relish and savour in it of the things of God. When his tribulations did abound, his consolations and experiences did much more abound, whence we may observe that the afflictive exercises of God's people, and particularly of his ministers, often tend to the advantage of others as well as to their own. The apostle's design is to settle and establish the Ephesians in the truth, and further to acquaint them with the mystery of the gospel, in order to it. In the former part he represents the great privilege of the Ephesians, who, having been in time past idolatrous heathens, were now converted to Christianity and received into covenant with God, which he illustrates from a view of their deplorable state before their conversion, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.1-Eph.3.21">ch. 1-3</reference>. In the latter part (which we have in the <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1-Eph.6.24">4th, 5th, and 6th chapters</reference>) he instructs them in the principal duties of religion, both personal and relative, and exhorts and quickens them to the faithful discharge of them. Zanchy observes that we have here an epitome of the whole Christian doctrine, and of almost all the chief heads of divinity. <div eID="gen31798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31799" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31800" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The introduction to the whole epistle, which is much the same as in others, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.1-Eph.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The apostle's thanksgivings and praises to God for his inestimable blessings bestowed on the believing Ephesians, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3-Eph.1.14">ver. 3-14</reference>. III. His earnest prayers to God in their behalf, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15-Eph.1.23">ver. 15-23</reference>. This great apostle was wont to abound in prayers and in thanksgivings to almighty God, which he generally so disposes and orders that at the same time they carry with them and convey the great and important doctrines of the Christian religion, and the most weighty instructions to all those who seriously peruse them. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv116"/> <div eID="gen31800" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31799" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Introduction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31801" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus: <hi type="super">2</hi> Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> to you, and peace, from God our Father, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen31801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31802" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The title St. Paul takes to himself, as belonging to him—<hi type="italic">Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ,</hi> &c. He reckoned it a great honour to be employed by Christ, as one of his messengers to the sons of men. The apostles were prime officers in the Christian church, being extraordinary ministers appointed for a time only. They were furnished by their great Lord with extraordinary gifts and the immediate assistance of the Spirit, that they might be fitted for publishing and spreading the gospel and for governing the church in its infant state. Such a one Paul was, and that not <hi type="italic">by the will</hi> of man conferring that office upon him, nor by his own intrusion into it; but <hi type="italic">by the will of God,</hi> very expressly and plainly intimated to him, he being immediately called (as the other apostles were) by Christ himself to the work. Every faithful minister of Christ (though his call and office are not of so extraordinary a nature) may, with our apostle, reflect on it as an honour and comfort to himself that he is what he is <hi type="italic">by the will of God.</hi> 2. The persons to whom this epistle is sent: <hi type="italic">To the saints who are at Ephesus,</hi> that is, to the Christians who were members of the church at Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia. He calls them saints, for such they were in profession, such they were bound to be in truth and reality, and many of them were such. All Christians must be saints; and, if they come not under that character on earth, they will never be saints in glory. He calls them <hi type="italic">the faithful in Christ Jesus,</hi> believers in him, and firm and constant in their adherence to him and to his truths and ways. Those are not saints who are not faithful, believing in Christ, firmly adhering to him, and true to the profession they make of relation to their Lord. Note, It is the honour not only of ministers, but of private Christians too, to have obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful.—<hi type="italic">In Christ Jesus,</hi> from whom they derive all their grace and spiritual strength, and in whom their persons, and all that they perform, are made accepted. 3. The apostolical benediction: <hi type="italic">Grace be to you,</hi> &c. This is the token in every epistle; and it expresses the apostle's good-will to his friends, and a real desire of their welfare. By <hi type="italic">grace</hi> we are to understand the free and undeserved love and favour of God, and those graces of the Spirit which proceed from it; by <hi type="italic">peace</hi> all other blessings, spiritual and temporal, the fruits and product of the former. No peace without grace. No peace, nor grace, but <hi type="italic">from God the Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> These peculiar blessings proceed from God, not as a Creator, but as a Father by special relation: and they come from our Lord Jesus Christ, who, having purchased them for his people, has a right to bestow them upon them. Indeed the saints, and the faithful in Christ Jesus, had already received grace and peace; but the increase of these is very desirable, and the best saints stand in need of fresh supplies of the graces of the Spirit, and cannot but desire to improve and grow: and therefore they should pray, each one for himself and all for one another, that such blessings may still abound unto them. <div eID="gen31802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31803" type="x-p"/> After this short introduction he comes to the matter and body of the epistle; and, though it may seem somewhat peculiar in a letter, yet the Spirit of God saw fit that his discourse of divine things in this chapter should be cast into prayers and praises, which, as they are solemn addresses to God, so they convey weighty instructions to others. Prayer may preach; and praise may do so too.
entries.a047b47b864bc0259f15596386640f7d675735dc: <div eID="gen31803" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Praise for Spiritual Blessings. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly <hi type="italic">places</hi> in Christ: <hi type="super">4</hi> According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: <hi type="super">5</hi> Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, <hi type="super">6</hi> To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. <hi type="super">7</hi> In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace; <hi type="super">8</hi> Wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence; <hi type="super">9</hi> Having made known unto us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he hath purposed in himself: <hi type="super">10</hi> That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; <hi type="italic">even</hi> in him: 11 In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will: <hi type="super">12</hi> That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first trusted in Christ. <hi type="super">13</hi> In whom ye also <hi type="italic">trusted,</hi> after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, <hi type="super">14</hi> Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory. <div eID="gen31804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31805" type="x-p"/> He begins with thanksgivings and praise, and enlarges with a great deal of fluency and copiousness of affection upon the exceedingly great and precious benefits which we enjoy by Jesus Christ. For the great privileges of our religion are very aptly recounted and enlarged upon in our praises to God. <div eID="gen31805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31806" type="x-p"/> I. In general he blesses God for <hi type="italic">spiritual blessings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">v. 3</reference>, where he styles him <hi type="italic">the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ;</hi> for, as Mediator, the Father was his God; as God, and the second person in the blessed Trinity, God was his Father. It bespeaks the mystical union between Christ and believers, that the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is their God and Father, and that in and through him. All blessings come from God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. No good can be expected from a righteous and holy God to sinful creatures, but by his mediation. <hi type="italic">He hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings.</hi> Note, Spiritual blessings are the best blessings with which God blesses us, and for which we are to bless him. He blesses us by bestowing such things upon us as make us really blessed. We cannot thus bless God again; but must do it by praising, and magnifying, and speaking well of him on that account. Those whom God blesses with some he blesses with all spiritual blessings; to whom he gives Christ, he freely gives all these things. It is not so with temporal blessings; some are favoured with health, and not with riches; some with riches, and not with health, &c. But, where God blesses with spiritual blessings, he blesses with all. They are <hi type="italic">spiritual blessings in heavenly places;</hi> that is, say some, in the church, distinguished from the world, and called out of it. Or it may be read, <hi type="italic">in heavenly things,</hi> such as come from heaven, and are designed to prepare men for it, and to secure their reception into it. We should hence learn to mind spiritual and heavenly things as the principal things, spiritual and heavenly blessings as the best blessings, with which we cannot be miserable and without which we cannot but be so. <hi type="italic">Set not your affections on things on the earth, but on those things which are above.</hi> These we are blessed with in Christ; for, as all our services ascend to God through Christ, so all our blessings are conveyed to us in the same way, he being the Mediator between God and us. <div eID="gen31806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31807" type="x-p"/> II. The particular spiritual blessings with which we are blessed in Christ, and for which we ought to bless God, are (many of them) here enumerated and enlarged upon. 1. Election and predestination, which are the secret springs whence the others flow, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4-Eph.1.5">v. 4, 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Election,</hi> or choice, respects that lump or mass of mankind out of which some are chosen, from which they are separated and distinguished. Predestination has respect to the blessings they are designed for; particularly <hi type="italic">the adoption of children,</hi> it being the purpose of God that in due time we should become his adopted children, and so have a right to all the privileges and to the inheritance of children. We have here the date of this act of love: it was <hi type="italic">before the foundation of the world;</hi> not only before God's people had a being, but before the world had a beginning; for they were chosen in the counsel of God from all eternity. It magnifies these blessings to a high degree that they are the products of eternal counsel. The alms which you give to beggars at your doors proceed from a sudden resolve; but the provision which a parent makes for his children is the result of many thoughts, and is put into his last will and testament with a great deal of solemnity. And, as this magnifies divine love, so it secures the blessings to God's elect; for <hi type="italic">the purpose of God according to election shall stand.</hi> He acts in pursuance of his eternal purpose in bestowing spiritual blessings upon his people. <hi type="italic">He hath blessed us</hi>—<hi type="italic">according as he hath chosen us in him,</hi> in Christ the great head of the election, who is emphatically called <hi type="italic">God's elect, his chosen;</hi> and in the chosen Redeemer an eye of favour was cast upon them. Observe here one great end and design of this choice: <hi type="italic">chosen—that we should be holy;</hi> not because he foresaw they would be holy, but because he determined to make them so. All who are chosen to happiness as the end are chosen to holiness as the means. Their sanctification, as well as their salvation, is the result of the counsels of divine love.—<hi type="italic">And without blame before him</hi>—that their holiness might not be merely external and in outward appearance, so as to prevent blame from men, but internal and real, and what God himself, who <hi type="italic">looketh at the heart,</hi> will account such, such holiness as proceeds from love to God and to our fellow-creatures, this charity being the principle of all true holiness. The original word signifies such an innocence as no man can carp at; and therefore some understand it of that perfect holiness which the saints shall attain in the life to come, which will be eminently before God, they being in his immediate presence for ever. Here is also the rule and the fontal cause of God's election: it is <hi type="italic">according to the good pleasure of his will</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">v. 5</reference>), not for the sake of any thing in them foreseen, but because it was his sovereign will, and a thing highly pleasing to him. It is <hi type="italic">according to the purpose,</hi> the fixed and unalterable will, <hi type="italic">of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">v. 11</reference>), who powerfully accomplishes whatever concerns his elect, as he has wisely and freely fore-ordained and decreed, the last and great end and design of all which is his own glory: <hi type="italic">To the praise of the glory of his grace (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">v. 6</reference>), that we should be to the praise of his glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.12">v. 12</reference>), that is, that we should live and behave ourselves in such a manner that his rich grace might be magnified, and appear glorious, and worthy of the highest praise. <hi type="italic">All is of God, and from him, and through him,</hi> and therefore all must be to him, and centre in his praise. Note, The glory of God is his own end, and it should be ours in all that we do. This passage has been understood by some in a very different sense, and with a special reference to the conversion of these Ephesians to Christianity. Those who have a mind to see what is said to this purpose may consult Mr. Locke, and other well-known writers, on the place. 2. The next spiritual blessing the apostle takes notice of is acceptance with God through Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">Wherein,</hi> or by which grace, <hi type="italic">he hath made us accepted in the beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">v. 6</reference>. Jesus Christ is the beloved of his Father (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>), as well as of angels and saints. It is our great privilege to be accepted of God, which implies his love to us and his taking us under his care and into his family. We cannot be thus accepted of God, but in and through Jesus Christ. He loves his people for the sake of the beloved. 3. Remission of sins, and redemption through the blood of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">v. 7</reference>. No remission without redemption. It was by reason of sin that we were captivated, and we cannot be released from our captivity but by the remission of our sins. This redemption we have in Christ, and this remission through his blood. The guilt and the stain of sin could be no otherwise removed than by the blood of Jesus. All our spiritual blessings flow down to us in that stream. This great benefit, which comes freely to us, was dearly bought and paid for by our blessed Lord; and yet it is according to the riches of God's grace. Christ's satisfaction and God's rich grace are very consistent in the great affair of man's redemption. God was satisfied by Christ as our substitute and surety; but it was rich grace that would accept of a surety, when he might have executed the severity of the law upon the transgressor, and it was rich grace to provide such a surety as his own Son, and freely to deliver him up, when nothing of that nature could have entered into our thoughts, nor have been any otherwise found out for us. In this instance he has not only manifested riches of grace, but <hi type="italic">has abounded towards us in all wisdom and prudence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">v. 8</reference>), wisdom in contriving the dispensation, and prudence in executing the counsel of his will, as he has done. How illustrious have the divine wisdom and prudence rendered themselves, in so happily adjusting the matter between justice and mercy in this grand affair, in securing the honour of God and his law, at the same time that the recovery of sinners and their salvation are ascertained and made sure! 4. Another privilege which the apostle here blesses God for is divine revelation—that God hath <hi type="italic">made known to us the mystery of his will</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">v. 9</reference>), that is, so much of his good-will to men, which had been concealed for a long time, and is still concealed from so great a part of the world: this we owe to Christ, who, having lain in the bosom of the Father from eternity, came to declare his will to the children of men. <hi type="italic">According to his good pleasure,</hi> his secret counsels concerning man's redemption, <hi type="italic">which he had purposed,</hi> or resolved upon, merely in and from himself, and not for any thing in them. In this revelation, and in his <hi type="italic">making known unto us the mystery of his will,</hi> the wisdom and the prudence of God do abundantly shine forth. It is described (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">v. 13</reference>) <hi type="italic">as the word of truth, and the gospel of our salvation.</hi> Every word of it is true. It contains and instructs us in the most weighty and important truths, and it is confirmed and sealed by the very oath of God, whence we should learn to <hi type="italic">betake ourselves to it in all our searches after divine truth.</hi> It is the gospel of our salvation: it publishes the glad tidings of salvation, and contains the offer of it: it points out the way that leads to it; and the blessed Spirit renders the reading and the ministration of it effectual to the salvation of souls. O, how ought we to prize this glorious gospel and to bless God for it! This is the light shining in a dark place, for which we have reason to be thankful, and to which we should take heed. 5. Union in and with Christ is a great privilege, a spiritual blessing, and the foundation of many others. <hi type="italic">He gathers together in one all things in Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">v. 10</reference>. All the lines of divine revelation meet in Christ; all religion centres in him. Jews and Gentiles were united to each other by being both united to Christ. <hi type="italic">Things in heaven and things on earth</hi> are gathered together in him; peace made, correspondence settled, between heaven and earth, through him. The innumerable company of angels become one with the church through Christ: this God <hi type="italic">purposed in himself,</hi> and it was his design in that dispensation which was to be accomplished by his sending Christ in the fulness of time, at the exact time that God had prefixed and settled. 6. The eternal inheritance is the great blessing with which we are blessed in Christ: <hi type="italic">In whom also we have obtained an inheritance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">v. 11</reference>. Heaven is the inheritance, the happiness of which is a sufficient portion for a soul: it is conveyed in the way of an inheritance, being the gift of a Father to his children. <hi type="italic">If children, then heirs.</hi> All the blessings that we have in hand are but small if compared with the inheritance. What is laid out upon an heir in his minority is nothing to what is reserved for him when he comes to age. Christians are said to have obtained this inheritance, as they have a present right to it, and even actual possession of it, in Christ their head and representative. 7. The seal and earnest of the Spirit are of the number of these blessings. We are said to be <hi type="italic">sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">v. 13</reference>. The blessed Spirit is holy himself, and he makes us holy. He is called <hi type="italic">the Spirit of promise,</hi> as he is the promised Spirit. By him believers are sealed; that is, separated and set apart for God, and distinguished and marked as belonging to him. The Spirit <hi type="italic">is the earnest of our inheritance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">v. 14</reference>. The earnest is part of payment, and it secures the full sum: so is the gift of the Holy Ghost; all his influences and operations, both as a sanctifier and a comforter, are heaven begun, glory in the seed and bud. The Spirit's illumination is an earnest of everlasting light; sanctification is an earnest of perfect holiness; and his comforts are earnests of everlasting joys. He is said to be the earnest, <hi type="italic">until the redemption of the purchased possession.</hi> It may be called here the possession, because this earnest makes it as sure to the heirs as though they were already possessed of it; and it is purchased for them by the blood of Christ. The redemption of it is mentioned because it was mortgaged and forfeited by sin; and Christ restores it to us, and so is said to redeem it, in allusion to the law of redemption. Observe, from all this, what a gracious promise that is which secures the gift of the Holy Ghost to those who ask him. <div eID="gen31807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31808" type="x-p"/> The apostle mentions the great end and design of God in bestowing all these spiritual privileges, <hi type="italic">that we should be to the praise of his glory who first trusted in Christ</hi>—we to whom the gospel was first preached, and who were first converted to the faith of Christ, and to the placing of our hope and trust in him. Note, Seniority in grace is a preferment: <hi type="italic">Who were in Christ before me,</hi> says the apostle (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Rom. xvi. 7</reference>); those who have for a longer time experienced the grace of Christ are under more special obligations to glorify God. They should be strong in faith, and more eminently glorify him; but this should be the common end of all. For this we were made, and for this we were redeemed; this is the great design of our Christianity, and of God in all that he has done for us: <hi type="italic">unto the praise of his glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">v. 14</reference>. He intends that his grace and power and other perfection should by this means become conspicuous and illustrious, and that the sons of men should magnify him.
entries.50ec65cf89d66f5f83b71aad080cbeb1a41eac56: <div eID="gen31808" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 61.)</title> <div sID="gen31809" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Wherefore I also, after I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints, <hi type="super">16</hi> Cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers; 17 That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him: <hi type="super">18</hi> The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, 19 And what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power, <hi type="super">20</hi> Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set <hi type="italic">him</hi> at his own right hand in the heavenly <hi type="italic">places,</hi> <hi type="super">21</hi> Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: <hi type="super">22</hi> And hath put all <hi type="italic">things</hi> under his feet, and gave him <hi type="italic">to be</hi> the head over all <hi type="italic">things</hi> to the church, <hi type="super">23</hi> Which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all. <div eID="gen31809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31810" type="x-p"/> We have come to the last part of this chapter, which consists of Paul's earnest prayer to God in behalf of these Ephesians. We should pray for the persons for whom we give thanks. Our apostle blesses God for what he had done for them, and then he prays that he would do more for them. He gives thanks for spiritual blessings, and prays for further supplies of them; for God <hi type="italic">will for this be enquired of by the house of Israel, to do it for them.</hi> He has laid up these spiritual blessings for us in the hands of his Son, the Lord Jesus; but then he has appointed us to draw them out, and fetch them in, by prayer. We have no part nor lot in the matter, any further than we claim it by faith and prayer. One inducement to pray for them was the good account he had of them, <hi type="italic">of their faith in the Lord Jesus and love to all the saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15">v. 15</reference>. Faith in Christ, and love to the saints, will be attended with all other graces. Love to the saints, as such, and because they are such, must include love to God. Those who love saints, as such, love all saints, how weak in grace, how mean in the world, how fretful and peevish soever, some of them may be. Another inducement to pray for them was because they had received the earnest of the inheritance: this we may observe from the words being connected with the preceding ones by the particle <hi type="italic">wherefore.</hi> "Perhaps you will think that, having received the earnest, it should follow, therefore you are happy enough, and need take no further care: you need not pray for yourselves, nor I for you." No, quite the contrary. <hi type="italic">Wherefore—I cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.16">v. 16</reference>. While he blesses God for giving them the Spirit, he ceases not to pray that he would give unto them the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">v. 17</reference>), that he would give greater measures of the Spirit. Observe, Even the best of Christians need to be prayed for: and, while we hear well of our Christian friends, we should think ourselves obliged to intercede with God for them, that they may abound and increase yet more and more. Now what is it that Paul prays for in behalf of the Ephesians? Not that they might be freed from persecution; nor that they might possess the riches, honours, or pleasures of the world; but the great thing he prays for is the illumination of their understandings, and that their knowledge might increase and abound: he means it of a practical and experimental knowledge. The graces and comforts of the Spirit are communicated to the soul by the enlightening of the understanding. In this way he gains and keeps possession. Satan takes a contrary way: he gets possession by the senses and passions, Christ by the understanding. Observe, <div eID="gen31810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31811" type="x-p"/> I. Whence this knowledge must come from <hi type="italic">the God of our Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">v. 17</reference>. The Lord <hi type="italic">is a God of knowledge,</hi> and there is no sound saving knowledge but what comes from him; and therefore to him we must look for it, who is <hi type="italic">the God of our Lord Jesus Christ</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">v. 3</reference>) <hi type="italic">and the Father of glory.</hi> It is a Hebraism. God is infinitely glorious in himself all glory is due to him from his creatures, and he is the author of all that glory with which his saints are or shall be invested. Now he gives knowledge by giving the Spirit of knowledge; for the Spirit of God is the teacher of the saints, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of wisdom and revelation.</hi> We have the revelation of the Spirit in the word: but will that avail us, if we have not the wisdom of the Spirit in the heart? If the same Spirit who indited the sacred scriptures do not take the veil from off our hearts, and enable us to understand and improve them, we shall be never the better.—<hi type="italic">In the knowledge of him,</hi> or for the acknowledgment of him; not only a speculative knowledge of Christ, and of what relates to him, but an acknowledgment of Christ's authority by an obedient conformity to him, which must be by the help of <hi type="italic">the Spirit of wisdom and revelation.</hi> This knowledge is first in the understanding. He prays that <hi type="italic">the eyes of their understanding may be enlightened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">v. 18</reference>. Observe, Those who have their eyes opened, and have some understanding in the things of God, have need to be more and more enlightened, and to have their knowledge more clear, and distinct, and experimental. Christians should not think it enough to have warm affections, but they should labour to have clear understandings; they should be ambitious of being knowing Christians, and judicious Christians. <div eID="gen31811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31812" type="x-p"/> II. What it is that he more particularly desire they should grow in the knowledge of. 1. <hi type="italic">The hope of his calling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">v. 18</reference>. Christianity is our calling. God has called us to it, and on that account it is said to be his calling. There is a hope in this calling; for those who deal with God deal upon trust. And it is a desirable thing to know what this hope of our calling is, to have such an acquaintance with the immense privileges of God's people, and the expectations they have from God, and with respect to the heavenly world, as to be quickened thereby to the utmost diligence and patience in the Christian course. We ought to labour after, and pray earnestly for, a clearer insight into, and a fuller acquaintance with, the great objects of a Christian's hopes. 2. <hi type="italic">The riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints.</hi> Besides the heavenly inheritance prepared for the saints, there is a present inheritance in the saints; for grace is glory begun, and holiness is happiness in the bud. There is a glory in this inheritance, riches of glory, rendering the Christian more excellent and more truly honourable than all about him: and it is desirable to know this experimentally, to be acquainted with the principles, pleasures, and powers, of the spiritual and divine life. It may be understood of the glorious inheritance in or among the saints in heaven, where God does, as it were, lay forth all his riches, to make them happy and glorious, and where all that the saints are in possession of is transcendently glorious, as the knowledge that can be attained of this upon earth is very desirable, and must be exceedingly entertaining and delightful. Let us endeavour then, by reading, contemplation, and prayer, to know as much of heaven as we can, that we may be desiring and longing to be there. 3. <hi type="italic">The exceeding greatness of God's power towards those who believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">v. 19</reference>. The practical belief of the all-sufficiency of God, and of the omnipotence of divine grace, is absolutely necessary to a close and steady walking with him. It is a desirable thing to know experimentally the mighty power of that grace beginning and carrying on the work of faith in our souls. It is a difficult thing to bring a soul to believe in Christ, and to venture its all upon his righteousness, and upon the hope of eternal life. It is nothing less than an almighty power that will work this in us. The apostle speaks here with a mighty fluency and copiousness of expression, and yet, at the same time, as if he wanted words to express the <hi type="italic">exceeding greatness of God's almighty power,</hi> that power which God exerts towards his people, and by which <hi type="italic">he raised Christ from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">v. 20</reference>. That indeed was the great proof of the truth of the gospel to the world: but the transcript of that in ourselves (our sanctification, and rising from the death of sin, in conformity to Christ's resurrection) is the great proof to us. Though this cannot prove the truth of the gospel to another who knows nothing of the matter (there the resurrection of Christ is the proof), yet to be able to speak experimentally, as the Samaritans, "<hi type="italic">We have heard him ourselves,</hi> we have felt a mighty change in our hearts," will make us able to say, with the fullest satisfaction, <hi type="italic">Now we believe, and are sure, that this is the Christ, the Son of God.</hi> Many understand the apostle here as speaking of that <hi type="italic">exceeding greatness of power</hi> which God will exert for raising the bodies of believers to eternal life, even the same <hi type="italic">mighty power which he wrought in Christ when he raised him,</hi> &c. And how desirable a thing must it be to become at length acquainted with that power, by being raised out of the grave thereby unto eternal life! <div eID="gen31812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31813" type="x-p"/> Having said something of Christ and his resurrection, the apostle digresses a little from the subject he is upon to make some further honourable mention of the Lord Jesus and his exaltation. He sits at the Father's <hi type="italic">right hand in the heavenly places,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20-Eph.1.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. Jesus Christ is advanced above all, and he is set in authority over all, they being made subject to him. All the glory of the upper world, and all the powers of both worlds, are entirely devoted to him. The Father <hi type="italic">hath put all things under his feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">v. 22</reference>), according to the promise, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. All creatures whatsoever are in subjection to him; they must either yield him sincere obedience or fall under the weight of his sceptre, and receive their doom from him. God <hi type="small-caps">gave</hi> <hi type="italic">him to be head over all things.</hi> It was a gift to Christ, considered as a Mediator, to be advanced to such dominion and headship, and to have such a mystical body prepared for him: and it was a gift to the church, to be provided with a head endued with so much power and authority. God <hi type="italic">gave him to be the head over all things.</hi> He gave him all power both in heaven and in earth. <hi type="italic">The Father loves the Son, and hath given</hi> <hi type="small-caps">all</hi> <hi type="italic">things into his hands.</hi> But that which completes the comfort of this is that he is the head over all things to the church; he is entrusted with all power, that is, that he may dispose of all the affairs of the providential kingdom in subserviency to the designs of his grace concerning his church. With this therefore we may answer the messengers of the nations, that the Lord hath founded Zion. The same power that supports the world support the church; and we are sure he loves his church, for it <hi type="italic">is his body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.23">v. 23</reference>), his mystical body, and he will care for it. It is <hi type="italic">the fulness of him that filleth all in all.</hi> Jesus Christ filleth all in all; he supplies all defects in all his members, filling them with his Spirit, and even with <hi type="italic">the fulness of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">ch. iii. 19</reference>. And yet the church is said to be his fulness, because Christ as Mediator would not be complete if he had not a church. How could he be a king if he had not a kingdom? This therefore comes in to the honour of Christ, <hi type="italic">as Mediator, that the church is his fulness.</hi>  <chapter eID="Eph.1"/> <div eID="gen31813" type="x-p"/>

entries.2e96bb67a1b28995bd7cd22716dd0bfed72c1a3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17571"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> The headings (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Ep 1:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, show that this Epistle claims to be that of Paul. This claim is confirmed by the testimonies of Irenæus, [Against Heresies, 5.2,3; 1.8,5]; Clement of Alexandria, [Miscellanies, 4, P. 65, and The Instructor, 1.8]; Origen, [Against Celsus, 4,211]. It is quoted by Valentinus, A.D. 120, namely, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.18">Ep 3:14-18</reference>, as we know from Hippolytus [The Refutation of All Heresies, p. 193]. Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 12], testifies to its canonicity. So Tertullian [Against Marcion, 5,17]. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 12], which alludes to the frequent and affectionate mention made by Paul of the Christian state, privileges, and persons of the Ephesians in his Epistle.<div eID="gen35347" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35346" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> Two theories, besides the ordinary one, have been held on the question, to whom the Epistle is addressed. Grotius, after the heretic Marcion, maintains that it was addressed to the Church at Laodicea, and that it is the Epistle to which Paul refers in <reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>. But the Epistle to the Colossians was probably written before that to the Ephesians, as appears from the parallel passages in Ephesians bearing marks of being expanded from those in Colossians; and Marcion seems to have drawn his notion, as to our Epistle, from Paul's allusion (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>) to an Epistle addressed by him to the Laodiceans. Origen and Clement of Alexandria, and even Tertullian, who refers to Marcion, give no sanction to his notion. No single manuscript contains the heading, "to the saints that are at Laodicea." The very resemblance of the Epistle to the Ephesians, to that to the Colossians, is against the theory; for if the former were really the one addressed to Laodicea (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>), Paul would not have deemed it necessary that the churches of Colosse and Laodicea should interchange Epistles. The greetings, moreover (<reference osisRef="Col.4.15">Col 4:15</reference>), which he sends through the Colossians to the Laodiceans, are quite incompatible with the idea that Paul wrote an Epistle to the Laodiceans at the same time, and by the same bearer, Tychicus (the bearer of our Epistle to the Ephesians, as well as of that to Colosse, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>); for who, under such circumstances, would not send the greetings directly in the letter to the party saluted? The letter to Laodicea was evidently written some time before that to Colosse, Archbishop Usher has advanced the second theory: That it was an encyclical letter headed, as in Manuscript B., "to the saints that are ... and to the faithful," the name of each Church being inserted in the copy sent to it; and that its being sent to Ephesus first, occasioned its being entitled, as now, the Epistle to the Ephesians. Alford makes the following objections to this theory: (1) It is at variance with the spirit of the Epistle, which is clearly addressed to one set of persons throughout, co-existing in one place, and as one body, and under the same circumstances. (2) The improbability that the apostle, who in two of his Epistles (Second Corinthians and Galatians) has so plainly specified their encyclical character, should have here omitted such specification. (3) The still greater improbability that he should have, as on this hypothesis must be assumed, written a circular Epistle to a district, of which Ephesus was the commercial capital, addressed to various churches within that district, yet from its very contents (as by the opponents' hypothesis) not admitting of application to the Church of that metropolis, in which he had spent so long a time, and to which he was so affectionately bound. (4) The inconsistency of this hypothesis with the address of the Epistle, and the universal testimony of the ancient Church. The absence of personal greetings is not an argument for either of the two theories; for similarly there are none in Galatians, Philippians, First and Second Thessalonians, First Timothy. The better he knows the parties addressed, and the more general and solemn the subject, the less he seems to give of these individual notices. Writing, as he does in this Epistle, on the constitution and prospects of Christ's universal Church, he refers the Ephesians, as to personal matters, to the bearer of the Epistle, Tychicus (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">22</reference>). As to the omission of "which are at Ephesus" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Ep 1:1</reference>), in Manuscript B., so "in Rome" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>) is omitted in some old manuscripts: it was probably done by churches among whom it was read, in order to generalize the reference of its contents, and especially where the subject of the Epistle is catholic. The words are found in the margin of Manuscript B, from a first hand; and are found in all the oldest manuscripts and versions.<div eID="gen35348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> Paul's first visit to Ephesus (on the seacoast of Lydia, near the river Cayster) is related in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19-Acts.18.21">Ac 18:19-21</reference>. The work, begun by his disputations with the Jews in his short visit, was carried on by Apollos (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.24-Acts.18.26">Ac 18:24-26</reference>), and Aquila and Priscilla (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.26">Ac 18:26</reference>). At his second visit, after his journey to Jerusalem, and thence to the east regions of Asia Minor, he remained at Ephesus "three years" (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">Ac 19:10</reference>, the "two years" in which verse are only part of the time, and <reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>); so that the founding and rearing of this Church occupied an unusually large portion of the apostle's time and care; whence his language in this Epistle shows a warmth of feeling, and a free outpouring of thought, and a union in spiritual privileges and hope between him and them (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>, &c.), such as are natural from one so long and so intimately associated with those whom he addresses. On his last journey to Jerusalem, he sailed by Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Ephesian Church to meet him at Miletus, where he delivered his remarkable farewell charge (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.18-Acts.20.35">Ac 20:18-35</reference>).<div eID="gen35349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> This Epistle was addressed to the Ephesians during the early part of his imprisonment at Rome, immediately after that to the Colossians, to which it bears a close resemblance in many passages, the apostle having in his mind generally the same great truths in writing both. It is an undesigned proof of genuineness that the two Epistles, written about the same date, and under the same circumstances, bear a closer mutual resemblance than those written at distant dates and on different occasions. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.14">Col 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.2">Ep 3:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Ep 5:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">Ep 6:22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>; 2:5 with <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2-Eph.4.4">Ep 4:2-4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.12-Col.3.15">Col 3:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.16">Ep 4:16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.2.19">Col 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.32">Ep 4:32</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.13">Col 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22-Eph.4.24">Ep 4:22-24</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.6-Eph.5.8">Ep 5:6-8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.6-Col.3.8">Col 3:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.4">4</reference>; Ep 5:22-33; 6:1-9 with <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.24">Ep 4:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.25">25</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.9">Col 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.20-Eph.5.22">Ep 5:20-22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Col.3.17">Col 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">18</reference>. Tychicus and Onesimus were being sent to Colosse, the former bearing the two Epistles to the two churches respectively, the latter furnished with a letter of recommendation to Philemon, his former master, residing at Colosse. The date was probably about four years after his parting with the Ephesian elders at Miletus (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.6-Acts.20.38">Ac 20:6-38</reference>), about A.D. 62, before his imprisonment had become of the more severe kind, which appears in his Epistle to the Philippians. From <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference> it is plain he had at the time, though a prisoner, some degree of freedom in preaching, which accords with <reference osisRef="Acts.28.23">Ac 28:23</reference>, 30, 31, where he is represented as receiving at his lodgings all inquirers. His imprisonment began in February A.D. 61 and lasted "two whole years" (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.30">Ac 28:30</reference>) at least, and perhaps longer.<div eID="gen35350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> The Church of Ephesus was made up of converts partly from the Jews and partly from the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.8-Acts.19.10">Ac 19:8-10</reference>). Accordingly, the Epistle so addresses a Church constituted (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:14-22</reference>). Ephesus was famed for its idol temple of Artemis or Diana, which, after its having been burnt down by Herostratus on the night that Alexander the Great was born (355 B.C.), was rebuilt at enormous cost and was one of the wonders of the world. Hence, perhaps, have arisen his images in this Epistle drawn from a beautiful temple: the Church being in true inner beauty that which the temple of the idol tried to realize in outward show (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.19-Eph.2.22">Ep 2:19-22</reference>). The Epistle (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.17">Ep 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.1-Eph.5.13">5:1-13</reference>) implies the profligacy for which the Ephesian heathen were notorious. Many of the same expressions occur in the Epistle as in Paul's address to the Ephesian elders. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; 2:7, as to "grace," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Ac 20:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">32</reference>: this may well be called "the Epistle of the grace of God" [Alford]. Also, as to his "bonds," <reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>, and 4:1 with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.22">Ac 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.23">23</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>, as to "the counsel of God," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Ac 20:27</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>, as to "the redemption of the purchased possession," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>. Also <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; 2:20; 5:5, as to "building up" the "inheritance," with <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>.<div eID="gen35351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> The object of the Epistle is "to set forth the ground, the course, and the aim and end of THE Church of the Faithful in Christ. He speaks to the Ephesians as a type or sample of the Church universal" [Alford]. Hence, "the Church" throughout the Epistle is spoken of in the singular, not in the plural, "churches." The Church's foundation, its course, and its end, are his theme alike in the larger and smaller divisions of the whole Epistle. "Everywhere the foundation of the Church is in the will of the Father; the course of the Church is by the satisfaction of the Son; the end of the Church is the life in the Holy Spirit" [Alford]. Compare respectively <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>; 2:5; 3:16. This having been laid down as a matter of doctrine (this part closing with a sublime doxology, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.21">Ep 3:14-21</reference>), is then made the ground of practical exhortations. In these latter also (from <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>, onward), the same threefold division prevails, for the Church is represented as founded on the counsel of "God the Father, who is above all, through all, and in all," reared by the "one Lord," Jesus Christ, through the "one Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.4-Eph.4.6">Ep 4:4-6</reference>, &c.), who give their respective graces to the several members. These last are therefore to exercise all these graces in the several relations of life, as husbands, wives, servants, children, &c. The conclusion is that we must put on "the whole armor of God" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.13">Ep 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> The sublimity of the STYLE and LANGUAGE corresponds to the sublimity of the subjects and exceeds almost that of any part of his Epistles. It is appropriate that those to whom he so wrote were Christians long grounded in the faith. The very sublimity is the cause of the difficulty of the style, and of the presence of peculiar expressions occurring, not found elsewhere.<div eID="gen35353" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eph.1.1-Eph.1.23">Ep 1:1-23</reference>. Inscription: Origin of the Church in the Father's Eternal Counsel, and the Son's Bloodshedding: The Sealing of It by the Spirit. Thanksgiving and Prayer that They May Fully Know God's Gracious Power in Christ towards the Saints.</title> <div sID="gen35354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17571"/><hi type="bold">1. by--</hi>rather, "through the will of God": called to the apostleship through that same "will" which originated the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">9, 11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen35354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are at Ephesus--</hi>(See Introduction.)<div eID="gen35355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the saints ... and to the faithful--</hi>The same persons are referred to by both designations, as the Greek proves: "to those who are saints, and faithful in Christ Jesus." The sanctification by God is here put before man's faith. The twofold aspect of salvation is thus presented, God's grace in the first instance sanctifying us, (that is, setting us apart in His eternal purposes as holy unto Himself); and our faith, by God's gift, laying hold of salvation (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen35356" type="x-p"/>
entries.65c7f289298fe86969a11939a803f8700fb2031f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17572"/><div sID="gen35357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17572"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">1Co 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2Co 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.3">Ga 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen35357" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cc0838ab353efd77c99d352df470db6f59a72ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17573"/><div sID="gen35358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17573"/>3. The doxologies in almost all the Epistles imply the real sense of grace experienced by the writers and their readers (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>). <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3-Eph.1.14">Ep 1:3-14</reference> sets forth summarily the Gospel of the grace of God: the Father's work of love, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference> (choosing us to holiness, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; to sonship, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>; to acceptance, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>): the Son's, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference> (redemption, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>; knowledge of the mystery of His will, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>; an inheritance, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>); the Holy Spirit's, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference> (sealing, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>; giving an earnest of the inheritance, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the God and Father of ... Christ--</hi>and so the God and Father of us who are in Him (<reference osisRef="John.20.17">Joh 20:17</reference>). God is "the God" of the man Jesus, and "the Father" of the Divine Word. The Greek is, "Blessed us," not "hath blessed us"; referring to the past original counsel of God. As in creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.22">Ge 1:22</reference>) so in redemption (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>; Mt 5:3-11; 25:34) God "blesses" His children; and that not in mere words, but in acts.<div eID="gen35359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us--</hi>all Christians.<div eID="gen35360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blessings--</hi>Greek, "blessing." "All," that is, "every possible blessing for time and eternity, which the Spirit has to bestow" (so "spiritual" means; not "spiritual," as the term is now used, as opposed to bodily).<div eID="gen35361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in heavenly places--</hi>a phrase five times found in this Epistle, and not elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">6:12</reference>); Greek, "in the heavenly places." Christ's ascension is the means of introducing us into the heavenly places, which by our sin were barred against us. Compare the change made by Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.20">Ep 1:20</reference>). While Christ in the flesh was in the form of a servant, God's people could not realize fully their heavenly privileges as sons. Now "our citizenship (Greek) is in heaven" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>), where our High Priest is ever "blessing" us. Our "treasures" are there (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.20">Mt 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.6.21">21</reference>); our aims and affections (<reference osisRef="Col.3.1">Col 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>); our hope (<reference osisRef="Col.1.5">Col 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>); our inheritance (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1Pe 1:4</reference>). The gift of the Spirit itself, the source of the "spiritual blessing," is by virtue of Jesus having ascended thither (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ep 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen35362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>the center and source of all blessing to us. <div eID="gen35363" type="x-p"/>
entries.72f1cc4ebdff7bd256e32e8b956ef440041cdcc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17574"/><div sID="gen35364" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17574"/><hi type="bold">4. hath chosen us--</hi>Greek, "chose us out for Himself" (namely, out of the world, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>): referring to His original choice, spoken of as past.<div eID="gen35364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him--</hi>The repetition of the idea, "in Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>), implies the paramount importance of the truth that it is in Him, and by virtue of union to Him, the Second Adam, the Restorer ordained for us from everlasting, the Head of redeemed humanity, believers have all their blessings (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">Ep 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen35365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the foundation of the world--</hi>This assumes the eternity of the Son of God (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">Joh 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.24">24</reference>), as of the election of believers in Him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we should be holy--</hi>positively (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.2">De 14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen35367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without blame--</hi>negatively (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Ep 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen35368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before him--</hi>It is to Him the believer looks, walking as in His presence, before whom he looks to be accepted in the judgment (<reference osisRef="Col.1.22">Col 1:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Re 7:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in love--</hi>joined by Bengel and others with <reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>, "in love having predestinated us," &c. But English Version is better. The words qualify the whole clause, "that we should be holy ... before Him." Love, lost to man by the fall, but restored by redemption, is the root and fruit and sum of all holiness (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.12">1Th 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen35370" type="x-p"/>
entries.d925b66d1c8d367448e442648d1effe7c80603c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17575"/><div sID="gen35371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17575"/><hi type="bold">5. predestinated--</hi>more special in respect to the end and precise means, than "chosen" or elected. We are "chosen" out of the rest of the world; "predestinated" to all things that secure the inheritance for us (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>). "Foreordained."<div eID="gen35371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Jesus--</hi>Greek, "through Jesus."<div eID="gen35372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to himself--</hi>the Father (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). Alford explains, "adoption ... into Himself," that is, so that we should be partakers of the divine nature (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2Pe 1:4</reference>). Lachmann reads, "unto Him." The context favors the explanation of Calvin: God has regard to Himself and the glory of His grace (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.14">12, 14</reference>) as His ultimate end. He had one only-begotten Son, and He was pleased for His own glory, to choose out of a lost world many to become His adopted sons. Translate, "unto Himself."<div eID="gen35373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the good pleasure of his will--</hi>So the Greek (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.26">Mt 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Lu 10:21</reference>). We cannot go beyond "the good pleasure of His will" in searching into the causes of our salvation, or of any of His works (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Job.33.13">Job 33:13</reference>.) Why needest thou philosophize about an imaginary world of optimism? Thy concern is to take heed that thou be not bad. There was nothing in us which deserved His love (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Ep 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">9, 11</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen35374" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c52f02dc4986ec10ce281708459aab1f312f58c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17576"/><div sID="gen35375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17576"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>, 17, 18). The end aimed at (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Psa 50:23</reference>), that is, that the glory of His grace may be praised by all His creatures, men and angels.<div eID="gen35375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts read, "which." Then translate, "which He graciously bestowed on us." But English Version is supported by good manuscripts and the oldest versions.<div eID="gen35376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">us accepted--</hi>a kindred Greek word to "grace": charitos, echaritosen: translate, "graciously accepted"; "made us subjects of His grace"; "embraced us in the arms of His grace" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen35377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the beloved--</hi>pre-eminently so called (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.35">Joh 3:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>). Greek, "Son of His love." It is only "IN His Beloved" that He loves us (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen35378" type="x-p"/>
entries.753896bf86d69e084278587224f5dbb4d02b73ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17577"/><div sID="gen35379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17577"/><hi type="bold">7. In whom--</hi>"the Beloved" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>).<div eID="gen35379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have--</hi>as a present possession.<div eID="gen35380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redemption--</hi>Greek, "our (literally, 'the') redemption"; THE redemption which is the grand subject of all revelation, and especially of the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>), namely, from the power, guilt, and penal consequences of sin (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>). If a man were unable to redeem himself from being a bond-servant, his kinsman might redeem him (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.48">Le 25:48</reference>). Hence, antitypically the Son of God became the Son of man, that as our kinsman He might redeem us (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>). Another "redemption" follows, namely, that "of the purchased possession" hereafter (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.14">Ep 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen35381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through his blood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Ep 2:13</reference>); as the instrument; the propitiation, that is, the consideration (devised by His own love) for which He, who was justly angry (<reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Is 12:1</reference>), becomes propitious to us; the expiation, the price paid to divine justice for our sin (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Ro 3:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">1Co 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen35382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the forgiveness of sins--</hi>Greek, "the remission of our transgressions": not merely "pretermission," as the Greek (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Ro 3:25</reference>) ought to be translated. This "remission," being the explanation of "redemption," includes not only deliverance from sin's penalty, but from its pollution and enslaving power, negatively; and the reconciliation of an offended God, and a satisfaction unto a just God, positively.<div eID="gen35383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">riches of his grace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>); "the exceeding riches of His grace." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Ep 3:16</reference>, "according to the riches of His glory": so that "grace" is His "glory." <div eID="gen35384" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7e615914b47940321b30e206381469660b842ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17578"/><div sID="gen35385" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17578"/>8. Rather, "which He made to abound towards us."<div eID="gen35385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all wisdom and prudence--</hi>"wisdom" in devising the plan of redeeming mankind; "prudence" in executing it by the means, and in making all the necessary arrangements of Providence for that purpose. Paul attributes to the Gospel of God's grace "all" possible "wisdom and prudence," in opposition to the boasts of wisdom and prudence which the unbelieving Jews and heathen philosophers and false apostles arrogated for their teachings. Christ crucified, though esteemed "foolishness" by the world, is "the wisdom of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18-1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:18-30</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>, "the manifold wisdom of God." <div eID="gen35386" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c559adbabab631341b386092699de3155f88d9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17579"/><div sID="gen35387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17579"/>9. "He hath abounded," or "made (grace) to abound toward us" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">Ep 1:8</reference>), in that He made known to us, namely, experimentally, in our hearts.<div eID="gen35387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery--</hi>God's purpose of redemption hidden heretofore in His counsels, but now revealed (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">27</reference>). This "mystery" is not like the heathen mysteries, which were imparted only to the initiated few. All Christians are the initiated. Only unbelievers are the uninitiated.<div eID="gen35388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his good pleasure--</hi>showing the cause why "He hath made known to us the mystery," namely, His own loving "good pleasure" toward us; also the time and manner of His doing so, are according to His good pleasure.<div eID="gen35389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purposed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen35390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in himself--</hi>God the Father. Bengel takes it, "in Him," that is, Christ, as in <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>. But the proper name, "in Christ," <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>, immediately after, is inconsistent with His being here meant by the pronoun. <div eID="gen35391" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e71dc29b2598fbf721ab8fae195230f69cc163e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17580"/><div sID="gen35392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17580"/>10. Translate, "Unto the dispensation of the fulness of the times," that is, "which He purposed in Himself" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>) with a view to the economy of (the gracious administration belonging to) the fulness of the times (Greek, "fit times," "seasons"). More comprehensive than "the fulness of the time" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>). The whole of the Gospel times (plural) is meant, with the benefits to the Church dispensed in them severally and successively. Compare "the ages to come" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>). "The ends of the ages" (Greek, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">1Co 10:11</reference>); "the times (same Greek as here, 'the seasons,' or 'fitly appointed times') of the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.24">Lu 21:24</reference>); "the seasons which the Father hath put in His own power" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>); "the times of restitution of all things which God hath spoken by the prophets since the world began" (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.20">Ac 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.21">21</reference>). The coming of Jesus at the first advent, "in the fulness of time," was one of these "times." The descent of the Holy Ghost, "when Pentecost was fully come" (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Ac 2:1</reference>), was another. The testimony given by the apostles to Him "in due time" ("in its own seasons," Greek) (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>) was another. The conversion of the Jews "when the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled," the second coming of Christ, the "restitution of all things," the millennial kingdom, the new heaven and earth, shall be severally instances of "the dispensation of the fulness of the times," that is, "the dispensation of" the Gospel events and benefits belonging to their respective "times," when severally filled up or completed. God the Father, according to His own good pleasure and purpose, is the Dispenser both of the Gospel benefits and of their several fitting times (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen35392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather together in one--</hi>Greek, "sum up under one head"; "recapitulate." The "good pleasure which He purposed," was "to sum up all things (Greek, 'THE whole range of things') in Christ (Greek, 'the Christ,' that is, His Christ)" [Alford]. God's purpose is to sum up the whole creation in Christ, the Head of angels, with whom He is linked by His invisible nature, and of men with whom He is linked by His humanity; of Jews and Gentiles; of the living and the dead (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.15">Ep 3:15</reference>); of animate and inanimate creation. Sin has disarranged the creature's relation of subordination to God. God means to gather up all together in Christ; or as <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference> says, "By Him to reconcile all things unto Himself, whether things in earth or things in heaven." Alford well says, "The Church of which the apostle here mainly treats, is subordinated to Him in the highest degree of conscious and joyful union; those who are not His spiritually, in mere subjugation, yet consciously; the inferior tribes of creation unconsciously; but objectively, all are summed up in Him." <div eID="gen35393" type="x-p"/>
entries.516bd0ba15142ef51c071c8fbf4cec10d198efdf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17581"/><div sID="gen35394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17581"/><hi type="bold">11. In whom--</hi>by virtue of union to whom.<div eID="gen35394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">obtained an inheritance--</hi>literally, "We were made to have an inheritance" [Wahl]. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>, "His inheritance in the saints": as His inheritance is there said to be in them, so theirs is here said to be in Him (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Ac 26:18</reference>). However, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.12">Ep 1:12</reference>, "That we should BE TO ... His glory" (not "that we should have"), favors the translation of Bengel, Ellicott, and others, "We were made an inheritance." So the literal Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">De 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.29">9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">32:9</reference>). "Also" does not mean "we also," nor as English Version, "in whom also"; but, besides His having "made known to us His will," we were also "made His inheritance," or "we have also obtained an inheritance."<div eID="gen35395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">predestinated--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>). The foreordination of Israel, as the elect nation, answers to that of the spiritual Israelites, believers, to an eternal inheritance, which is the thing meant here. The "we" here and in <reference osisRef="Eph.1.12">Ep 1:12</reference>, means Jewish believers (whence the reference to the election of Israel nationally arises), as contrasted with "you" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>) Gentile believers.<div eID="gen35396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purpose--</hi>repeated from "purposed" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.11">Ep 3:11</reference>). The Church existed in the mind of God eternally, before it existed in creation.<div eID="gen35397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsel of his ... will--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.5">Ep 1:5</reference>), "the good pleasure of His will." Not arbitrary caprice, but infinite wisdom ("counsel") joined with sovereign will. Compare his address to the same Ephesians in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Ac 20:27</reference>, "All the counsel of God" (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Is 28:29</reference>). Alike in the natural and spiritual creations, God is not an agent constrained by necessity. "Wheresoever counsel is, there is election, or else it is vain; where a will, there must be freedom, or else it is weak" [Pearson]. <div eID="gen35398" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f83056487b103256e72a8cb248dfafe3f1624be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17582"/><div sID="gen35399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17582"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen35399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who first trusted in Christ--</hi>rather (we Jewish Christians), "who have before hoped in the Christ": who before the Christ came, looked forward to His coming, waiting for the consolation of Israel. Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.26.6">Ac 26:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.7">7</reference>, "I am judged for the hope of the promise made of God unto our fathers: unto which our twelve tribes, instantly serving God day and night, hope to come." <reference osisRef="Acts.28.20">Ac 28:20</reference>, "the hope of Israel" [Alford]. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; 2:12; 4:4. <div eID="gen35400" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3f7a5a7b9311d43f85482faacc3e13ba84e10d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17583"/><div sID="gen35401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17583"/><hi type="bold">13.
