The significance of a pledge lasts no longer than till both parties have fulfilled the bargain; and, accordingly, he afterwards adds, ye are sealed to the day of redemption, (Ephesians 4:30,) which means the day of judgment. Though we are now redeemed by the blood of Christ, the fruit of that redemption does not yet appear; for “every creature groaneth, desiring to be delivered from the bondage of corruption. And not only they, but ourselves also, who have the first-fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body;” for we have not yet obtained it, but by hope. (Romans 8:21-23.) But we shall obtain it in reality, when Christ shall appear to judgment. Such is the meaning of the word redemption in the passage now quoted from the Epistle to the Romans, and in a saying of our Lord,
“Look up, and lift up your heads, for your redemption draweth nigh.” (Luke 21:28.)
Περιποίησις, which we translate the possession obtained, is not the kingdom of heaven, or a blessed immortality, but the Church itself. This is added for their consolation, that they might not think it hard to cherish their hope till the day of Christ’s coming, or be displeased that they have not yet obtained the promised inheritance; for such is the common lot of the whole Church.
To the praise of his glory. The word praise, as in the twelfth verse, Ephesians 1:12 signifies “making known.”
“Louange yci se prend comme ci devant pour la publication et manifestation.” “Here, as formerly, ‘praise’ denotes proclamation and manifestation.”
The glory of God may sometimes be concealed, or imperfectly exhibited. But in the Ephesians God had given proofs of his goodness, that his glory might be celebrated and openly proclaimed. Those persons, therefore, who slighted the calling of the Ephesians, might be charged with envying and slighting the glory of God.
The frequent mention of the glory of God ought not to be regarded as superfluous, for what is infinite cannot be too strongly expressed. This is particularly true in commendations of the Divine mercy, for which every godly person will always feel himself unable to find adequate language. He will be more ready to utter, than other men will be to hear, the expression of praise; for the eloquence both of men and angels, after being strained to the utmost, falls immeasurably below the vastness of this subject. We may likewise observe, that there is not a more effectual method of shutting the mouths of wicked men, than by shewing that our views tend to illustrate, and theirs to obscure, the glory of God.
Ephesians 1:15-19
15. Wherefore I also, after I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and love unto all the saints,
15. Quapropter ego etiam, audita fide quae apud vos est in Domino Iesu, et charitate erga omnes sanctos,
16. Cease not to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers;
16. Non cesso gratias agere pro vobis, memoriam vestri faciens in orationibus meis;
17. That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him:
17. Ut Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Pater gloriae, det vobis Spiritum sapientiae et revelationis, in agnitione ipsius,
18. The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints,
18. Illuminatos oculos mentis vestrae, ut sciatis quae sit spes vocationis ipsius, et quae divitiae gloriae haereditatis ejus in sanctis,
19. And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power.
19. Et quae superexcellens magnitudo potentiae ejus erga nos, qui credidimus secundum efficaciam potentiae roboris ejus.
entries.1e77aa40799f38cf1ca745cec68ab5b2ffcbaf42: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.15" sID="gen124542" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">Wherefore I also.</hi> This thanksgiving was not simply an expression of his ardent love to the Ephesians. He congratulated them before God, that the opinion which he had formed respecting them was highly favorable. Observe here, that under <hi type="italic">faith and love</hi> Paul includes generally the whole excellence of Christian character. He uses the expression, <hi type="italic">faith in the Lord Jesus,</hi> <note n="117"> <div sID="gen124544" type="x-p"/> “‘Having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus.’ It is wrong to argue from this expression, with Olshausen and De Wette, that the apostle had no personal knowledge of the persons whom he addressed. This was an early surmise, for it is referred to by Theodoret. Some, says he, have supposed that the apostle wrote to the Ephesians, <foreign xml:lang="el">ὡς μηδέπω θεασάμενος αὐτοὺς</foreign>, (as having never seen them.) But some years had elapsed since the apostle had visited Ephesus, and seen the Ephesian Church; and might he not refer to reports of their Christian steadfastness which had reached him? Nay, his use of the word may signify that such intelligence had been repeatedly brought to him.” — Eadie.<div eID="gen124544" type="x-p"/> </note> because Christ is the aim and object of faith. <hi type="italic">Love</hi> ought to embrace all men, but here the <hi type="italic">saints</hi> are particularly mentioned; because love, when properly regulated, begins with them, and is afterwards extended to all others. If our love must have a view to God, the nearer any man approaches to God, the stronger unquestionably must be his claims to our love.<div eID="gen124543" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124542" osisID="Eph.1.15" type="section"/>
entries.636b72066dfe12faaa7f163f897d962ac699eaef: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.16" sID="gen124545" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">Making mention of you.</hi> To thanksgiving, as his custom is, he adds prayer, in order to excite them to additional progress. It was necessary that the Ephesians should understand that they had entered upon the proper course. But it was equally necessary that they should not turn aside to any new scheme of doctrine, or become indifferent about proceeding farther; for nothing is more dangerous than to be satisfied with that measure of spiritual benefits which has been already obtained. Whatever, then, may be the height of our attainments, let them be always accompanied by the desire of something higher.<div eID="gen124546" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124545" osisID="Eph.1.16" type="section"/>
entries.a355f521859c58ae17e3927af3a837eac087ec8d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.17" sID="gen124547" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> But what does Paul wish for the Ephesians? <hi type="italic">The spirit of wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the eyes of their understanding being enlightened.</hi> And did they not possess these? Yes; but at the same time they needed increase, that, being endowed with a larger measure of the Spirit, and being more and more enlightened, they might more clearly and fully hold their present views. The knowledge of the godly is never so pure, but that some dimness or obscurity hangs over their spiritual vision. But let us examine the words in detail.<div eID="gen124548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124549" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The God of our Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> The Son of God became man in such a manner, that God was his God as well as ours.<div eID="gen124549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124550" type="x-p"/>“I ascend,” says he, “to my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.20.17">John 20:17</reference>)<div eID="gen124550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124551" type="x-p"/>And the reason why he is our God, is, that he is the God of Christ, whose members we are. Let us remember, however, that this relates to his human nature; so that his subjection takes nothing away from his eternal godhead.<div eID="gen124551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124552" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The Father of glory.</hi> This title springs from the former; for God’s glory, as a Father, consists in subjecting his Son to our condition, that, through him, he might be our God. <hi type="italic">The Father of glory</hi> is a well-known Hebrew idiom for <hi type="italic">The glorious Father</hi>. There is a mode of pointing and reading this passage, which I do not disapprove, and which connects the two clauses in this manner: <hi type="italic">That God, the glorious Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, may give to you.</hi><div eID="gen124552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124553" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The Spirit of wisdom and revelation</hi> is here put, by a figure of speech, (metonymy,) for the grace which the Lord bestows upon us by his own Spirit. But let it be observed, that the gifts of the Spirit are not the gifts of nature. Till the Lord opens them, <hi type="italic">the eyes of our heart</hi> are blind. Till the Spirit has become our instructor, all that we know is folly and ignorance. Till the Spirit of God has made it known to us by a secret revelation, the knowledge of our Divine calling exceeds the capacity of our own minds.<div eID="gen124553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124554" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the knowledge of him.</hi> This might also be read, <hi type="italic">In the</hi> <hi type="italic">knowledge of himself</hi>. Both renderings agree well with the context, for he that knows the Son knows also the Father; but I prefer the former as more natively suggested by the Greek pronoun, ἐν ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ<div eID="gen124554" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124547" osisID="Eph.1.17" type="section"/>
entries.1365abaf9573a7508cc6570d48a4c68dce7bc04d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.18" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.18" sID="gen124555" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> <hi type="italic">The eyes of your understanding being enlightened.</hi> <hi type="italic">The</hi> <hi type="italic">eyes of your heart</hi> is the rendering of the Vulgate, which is supported by some Greek manuscripts. The difference is immaterial, for the Hebrews frequently employ it to denote the rational powers of the soul, though more strictly, being the seat of the affections, it means the will or desire; but I have preferred the ordinary translation.<div eID="gen124556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124557" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And what the riches.</hi> A comparison, suggested by its excellence, reminds us how unfit we are to receive this elevated knowledge; for the power of God is no small matter. This great power, he tells us, had been exerted, and in a very extraordinary manner, towards the Ephesians, who were thus laid under constant obligations to follow his calling. By thus extolling the grace of God toward themselves, he intended to check every tendency to despise or dislike the duties of the Christian life. But the splendid encomiums which he pronounces on faith convey to us also this instruction, that it is so admirable a work and gift of God, that no language can do justice to its excellence. Paul is not in the habit of throwing out hyperboles without discrimination; but when he comes to treat of a matter which lies so far beyond this world as faith does, he raises our minds to the admiration of heavenly power.<div eID="gen124557" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.18" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124555" osisID="Eph.1.18" type="section"/>
entries.42f1e1b710213c29058c428efa71b743a9526614:
19. According to the working. Some consider this clause as referring solely to the word believe, which comes immediately before it; but I rather view it as an additional statement, tending to heighten the greatness of the power, as a demonstration, or, if you prefer it, an instance and evidence of the efficacy of the power. The repetition of the word power, (δυνάμεως) has the appearance of being superfluous; but in the former case it is restricted to one class, — in the next, it has a general application. Paul, we find, never thinks that he can say enough in his descriptions of the Christian calling. And certainly the power of God is wonderfully displayed, when we are brought from death to life, and when, from being the children of hell, we become the children of God and heirs of eternal life.
Foolish men imagine that this language is absurdly hyperbolical; but godly persons, who are engaged in daily struggles with inward corruption, have no difficulty in perceiving that not a word is here used beyond what is perfectly just. As the importance of the subject cannot be too strongly expressed, so our unbelief and ingratitude led Paul to employ this glowing language. We never form adequate conceptions of the treasure revealed to us in the gospel; or, if we do, we cannot persuade ourselves that it is possible for us to do so, because we perceive nothing in us that corresponds to it, but everything the reverse. Paul’s object, therefore, was not only to impress the Ephesians with a deep sense of the value of Divine grace, but also to give them exalted views of the glory of Christ’s kingdom. That they might not be cast down by a view of their own unworthiness, he exhorts them to consider the power of God; as if he had said, that their regeneration was no ordinary work of God, but was an astonishing exhibition of his power.
According to the efficacy of the power of his strength. There are three words here, on which we may make a passing remark. We may view strength as the root, — power as the tree, — and efficacy as the fruit, or the stretching out of the Divine arm which terminates in action.
Ephesians 1:20-23
20. Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,
20. Quam exeruit in Christo, dum illum excitavit a mortuis, et sedere fecit in dextera sua, in coelestibus;
21. Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come;
21. Super omnem principatum, et potestatem, et virtutem, et dominationem, et omne nomen quod nominatur, non tantum in seculo hoc, sed etiam in futuro;
22. And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
22. Et omnia subjecit pedibus ejus, et ipsum posuit caput super omnia Ecclesiae,
23. Which is his body, the fullness of him that filleth all in all.
23. Quae est corpus ejus et complementum ejus, qui omnia in omnibus adimplet.
entries.c7cd1fa81dde1ab438b44a841c805acdf2771d29: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.20" sID="gen124573" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> <hi type="italic">Which he wrought in Christ.</hi> The Greek verb is ἐνέργησεν, from which ἐνέργεια is derived. It might run thus, <hi type="italic">According to</hi> <hi type="italic">the efficacy which he effected</hi>. But the translation which I have given conveys the same meaning, and is less harsh.<div eID="gen124574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124575" type="x-p"/>With the greatest propriety does he enjoin us to contemplate this power in Christ; for in us it is hitherto concealed. “My strength,” says he, “is made perfect in weakness.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.12.9">2 Corinthians 12:9</reference>.) In what do we excel the children of the world but in this, that our condition appears to be somewhat worse than theirs? Though sin does not reign, it continues to dwell in us, and death is still strong. Our blessedness, which lies in hope, is not perceived by the world. The power of the Spirit is a thing unknown to flesh and blood. A thousand distresses, to which we are daily liable, render us more despised than other men.<div eID="gen124575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124576" type="x-p"/>Christ alone, therefore, is the mirror in which we can contemplate that which the weakness of the cross hinders from being clearly seen in ourselves. When our minds rise to a confident anticipation of righteousness, salvation, and glory, let us learn to turn them to Christ. We still lie under the power of death; but he, raised from the dead by heavenly power, has the dominion of life. We labor under the bondage of sin, and, surrounded by endless vexations, are engaged in a hard warfare, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.18">1 Timothy 1:18</reference>;) but he, sitting at the right hand of the Father, exercises the highest government in heaven and earth, and triumphs gloriously over the enemies whom he has subdued and vanquished. We lie here mean and despised; but to him has been “given a name” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.9">Philippians 2:9</reference>,) which angels and men regard with reverence, and devils and wicked men with dread. We are pressed down here by the scantiness of all our comforts: but he has been appointed by the Father to be the sole dispenser of all blessings. For these reasons, we shall find our advantage in directing our views to Christ, that in him, as in a mirror, we may see the glorious treasures of Divine grace, and the unmeasurable greatness of that power, which has not yet been manifested in ourselves.<div eID="gen124576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124577" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And set him at his own right hand.</hi> This passage shews plainly, if any one does, what is meant by <hi type="italic">the right hand of God</hi>. It does not mean any particular place, but the power which the Father has bestowed on Christ, that he may administer in his name the government of heaven and earth. It is idle, therefore, to inquire why Stephen <hi type="italic">saw him standing,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.55">Acts 7:55</reference>,) while Paul describes him as <hi type="italic">sitting</hi> at God’s right hand. The expression does not refer to any bodily posture, but denotes the highest royal power with which Christ has been invested. This is intimated by what immediately follows, <hi type="italic">far above all principality and power:</hi> for the whole of this description is added for the purpose of explaining what is meant by<hi type="italic"> the right hand.</hi><div eID="gen124577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124578" type="x-p"/>God the Father is said to have raised Christ to “his right hand,” because he has made him to share in his government, because by him he exerts all his power; the metaphor being borrowed from earthly princes, who confer the honor of sitting along with themselves on those whom they have clothed with the highest authority. As the right hand of God fills heaven and earth, it follows that the kingdom and power of Christ are equally extensive. It is in vain, therefore, to attempt to prove that, because Christ sitteth at the right hand of God, he dwells in heaven alone. His human nature, it is true, resides in heaven, and not in earth; but that argument is foreign to the purpose. The expression which follows, <hi type="italic">in heavenly places,</hi> does not at all imply that the right hand of God is confined to heaven, but directs us to contemplate the heavenly glory amidst which our Lord Jesus dwells, the blessed immortality which he enjoys, and the dominion over angels to which he has been exalted.<div eID="gen124578" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124573" osisID="Eph.1.20" type="section"/>
entries.c61805d0bf33f620beeab9b4f53e74421c0dfeee: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.21" sID="gen124579" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> <hi type="italic">Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion.</hi> All these names, there can be no doubt, are applied to angels, who are so denominated, because, by means of them, God exercises his power, and might, and dominion. He permits them to share, as far as is competent to creatures, what belongs to himself, and even gives to them his own name; for we find that they are called <foreign xml:lang="he">אלהים</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">elohim,</hi>) <hi type="italic">gods</hi>. From the diversity of names we conclude that there are various orders of angels; but to attempt to settle these with exactness, to fix their number, or determine their ranks, would not merely discover foolish curiosity, but would be rash, wicked, and dangerous.<div eID="gen124580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124581" type="x-p"/>But why did he not simply call them Angels? I answer, it was to convey exalted views of the glory of Christ that Paul employed those lofty titles. As if he had said, “There is nothing so elevated or excellent, by whatever name it may be named, that is not subject to the majesty of Christ.” There was an ancient superstition, prevalent both among Jews and Gentiles, falsely attributing to angels many things, in order to draw away their minds from God himself, and from the true Mediator. Paul constantly labors to prevent this imaginary lustre of angels from dazzling the eyes of men, or obscuring the brightness of Christ; and yet his utmost exertions could not prevent “the wiles of the devil”(<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.11">Ephesians 6:11</reference>) from succeeding in this matter. Thus we see how the world, through a superstitious dread of angels, departed from Christ. It was indeed the unavoidable consequence of the false opinions entertained respecting angels, that the pure knowledge of Christ disappeared.<div eID="gen124581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen124582" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Above every name that is named.</hi> <hi type="italic">Name</hi> is here taken for largeness, or excellence; and <hi type="italic">to be named</hi> means to enjoy celebrity and praise. <hi type="italic">The age that is to come</hi> is expressly mentioned, to point out that the exalted rank of Christ is not temporal, but eternal; and that it is not limited to this world, but shines illustriously in the kingdom of God. For this reason, too, Isaiah calls him, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.6">Isaiah 9:6</reference>,) <hi type="italic">The Father of the future age</hi>. In short, the glories of men and angels are made to hold an inferior place, that the glory of Christ, unequalled and unapproached, may shine above them all.<div eID="gen124582" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124579" osisID="Eph.1.21" type="section"/>
entries.a107cfcd6dcbe59e9924b7c91b1e7917ce7b6f37: <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Eph.1.22" sID="gen124583" type="section"/> <div sID="gen124584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">And gave him to be the head.</hi> He was made the head of the Church, on the condition that he should have the administration of all things. The apostle shews that it was not a mere honorary title, but was accompanied by the entire command and government of the universe. The metaphor of a <hi type="italic">head</hi> denotes the highest authority. I am unwilling to dispute about a name, but we are driven to it by the base conduct of those who flatter the Romish idol. Since Christ alone is called “the head,” all others, whether angels or men, must rank as members; so that he who holds the highest place among his fellows is still one of the members of the same body. And yet they are not ashamed to make an open avowal that the Church will be ἀκέφαλον, <hi type="italic">without a head</hi>, if it has not another head on earth besides Christ. So small is the respect which they pay to Christ, that, if he obtain undivided that honor which his Father has bestowed upon him, the Church is supposed to be disfigured. This is the basest sacrilege. But let us listen to the Apostle, who declares that the Church is His body, and, consequently, that those who refuse to submit to Him are unworthy of its communion; for on Him alone the unity of the Church depends.<div eID="gen124584" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Eph.1.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen124583" osisID="Eph.1.22" type="section"/>
entries.a88dfde2483aff85cb96681d8564096ecc1ef2b6:
23. The fullness of him that filleth all in all. This is the highest honor of the Church, that, until He is united to us, the Son of God reckons himself in some measure imperfect. What consolation is it for us to learn, that, not until we are along with him, does he possess all his parts, or wish to be regarded as complete! Hence, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, [1Co 12:12-31] when the apostle discusses largely the metaphor of a human body, he includes under the single name of Christ the whole Church.
That filleth all in all. This is added to guard against the supposition that any real defect would exist in Christ, if he were separated from us. His wish to be filled, and, in some respects, made perfect in us, arises from no want or necessity; for all that is good in ourselves, or in any of the creatures, is the gift of his hand; and his goodness appears the more remarkably in raising us out of nothing, that he, in like manner, may dwell and live in us. There is no impropriety in limiting the word all to its application to this passage; for, though all things are regulated by the will and power of Christ, yet the subject of which Paul particularly speaks is the spiritual government of the Church. There is nothing, indeed, to hinder us from viewing it as referring to the universal government of the world; but to limit it to the case in hand is the more probable interpretation.
CHAPTER 2
Ephesians 2:1-3
1. And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
1. Et vos, quum essetis mortui delictis et peccatis vestris;
2. Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
2. In quibus aliquando ambulastis secundum saeculum mundi hujus, secundum principem potestatis aeris, spiritus scilicet, qui nunc operatur in filiis inobedientiae;
3. Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
3. Inter quos nos quoque omnes aliquando conversati sumus in concupiscentiis carnis nostrae, facientes quae carni libebant, et menti; et eramus natura filii irae, sicut et caeteri.

               <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 PAUL an apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 1.1. 2 Cor. 1.1.</ns0:note> to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithfull <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This may be understood either, 1. by way of Restric<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, of those that are sincere and constant to Christ, and so not onely Saints by profession, but true to their profes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion; or, 2. rather, by way of Explication: he defines those Saints he spake of, and calls them <ns0:hi>faithfull in Christ</ns0:hi> here, whom he called Saints before.</ns0:note> in Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Authour and Fountain of that holiness which denominates them Saints.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 1.2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 1.3.</ns0:note> Grace <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> to you, and peace from God our Father, and <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> the Lord Jesus Christ.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Cor. 1.3. 1 Pet. 1.3.</ns0:note> Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thanked, praised. We bless God when we praise him for, and acknowledge him in his excellencies or bene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fits.</ns0:note> the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Hath vouchsafed or communicated all spiritual Bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sings to us. God blesseth us when he doeth good to us; and so the word <ns0:hi>Bless</ns0:hi> is taken in a different sense from what it was in the former clause.</ns0:note> us with all <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of all sorts or kinds.</ns0:note> spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">In opposition to temporal and worldly, which the carnal <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> principally expected, and the Law mostly promised, (<ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28.1, 2. to v. 15.) and which were but types and shadows of those spiritual Blessings which immediately re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late to the spiritual Life and Salvation of Believers.</ns0:note> blessings in heavenly <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>things.</ns0:hi> Chap. 6.12.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>places</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Gr. <ns0:hi>Supercoelestial</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Heavenly,</ns0:hi> understand either, 1. <ns0:hi>Things</ns0:hi>; and then it seems to be the same as spiritual Blessings, onely in other terms. Or, 2. <ns0:hi>Places,</ns0:hi> in opposition to <ns0:hi>earthly</ns0:hi> Pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, particularly the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> in which God had formerly promised to Bless his people. These spiritual Blessings are in heavenly places, because, though they reach us here on earth, yet they are derived to us from God and Christ in Heaven, and in Heaven onely have their full per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection and consummation hereafter.</ns0:note> in Christ <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By, or through Christ. Upon the account of whose merit, and by whose efficiency these spiritual Blessings are derived from God to us. Or, in Christ as our head, the repository, and seat of all divine Blessings, from whom they flow down upon us as his Members, receiving all we have, out of his fullness. He seems to have respect to the promise made to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> Gen. 22.18. <ns0:hi>That in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed,</ns0:hi> pointing out Christ as that Seed, and those Blessings as Spiritual. <ns0:hi>Vid. Act.</ns0:hi> 3.25, 26.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 According <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">God blesseth us with all spiritual Blessings <ns0:hi>according</ns0:hi> as he hath chosen us; Election being the fountain from whence those Blessings come, so that God doeth nothing for us in carrying on the work of our Salvation, but what he had in his eternal council before determined.</ns0:note> as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Tim. 1.9.</ns0:note> he hath chosen us <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Separated us in his purpose and decree from others (whom he left out of that gracious act of his will) and determined that we should be holy and unblameable, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in him <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either, 1. as in the former verse, by, and through Christ, for his sake, and upon the account of his merit as the procuring cause, not of our E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lection, but Sanctification; <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> God hath chosen us, that we should be made holy and unblameable by Christ. Or, 2. rather, in Christ as the foundation on which he would build us (his spiritual house) and by which both we might be united to God, and he communicate his Influence and Grace to us; or as our head, by which he might convey grace, and strength, and life to us as Christ's Members.</ns0:note>, before the foundation of the world <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either before God's Decree of creating the World, or rather, before his executing that Decree in the actual crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of it, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> from Eternity, when, nor we, nor the world had a being.</ns0:note>, that we <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Col. 1.22.</ns0:note> should be holy and without blame <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">By inherent Grace begun in Regeneration, and carried on in Sanctification and Mortification in this life, though not perfected till the other. Holiness in us is declared here to be not the cause, but the effect of our E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lection: we are chosen that we may be holy, not because we are, or God foresees we will be holy.</ns0:note> before him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In the sight of God who is not deceived with an outward appearance, but looks to the Heart.</ns0:note> in love <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As a principal part of our Sanctifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation, and the best evidence of the fear of God in us, and our obedience to the whole Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 8.29, 30.</ns0:note> Having predestinated us to <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Rom. 8.15. Gal. 4.5.</ns0:note> the adopti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of children <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Having appointed us unto a state of Son-ship and right to Glory. This seems to be more than the former, a greater thing to be the Sons of God, and Heirs of Heaven, than to be Holy.</ns0:note> by Christ Jesus <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">As Mediatour, and Head of the Elect, and the foundation of all Spiritual Blessings vouchsafed them, and so of this relation into which they are brought, by being united to him. The adopted Children come into that state by the intervention of the natural Son.</ns0:note> to himself <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either, 1. <ns0:hi>in himself, i. e.</ns0:hi> looking no farther than to himself for the cause of, and motive to his adopting them. Or, 2. ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to our translation, <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> himself, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to God. Or, rather, 3. for himself, (as the <ns0:hi>Syriac</ns0:hi> renders it) God would have the honour of having many adopted children that should all call him Father.</ns0:note> ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the good pleasure of his will <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">His Sovereign grace and good will as the onely spring from which predestination issued, God being moved to it by nothing out of himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:485" />6 To the praise of the glory of his grace <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Glory of Grace, by an usual <ns0:hi>Hebraism,</ns0:hi> for glorious grace, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> large, abundant, admirable. The praise of this Grace the Apostle makes the end of God's chusing and predestinating us to the Adoption of Children. God hath chosen us, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and therein manifested his Grace to us, that such as it is in it self, such it may be aknowledged to be; and therefore praised and adored by us.</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> wherein <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>through,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> the same Grace out of which he chose us.</ns0:note> he hath made us accepted in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 3.17.</ns0:note> the beloved <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Having chosen us in Christ, he likewise favours us, is well pleased with us in Christ, to whom we are united, whose Members we are, and in whom God looks upon us. We are hatefull in our selves as Sinners, but accepted in Christ as Sons.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 20.28. Col. 1.14. Heb. 9.12. 1 Pet. 1.18.</ns0:note> In whom <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In Christ Godman the immediate worker of this Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demption; for though the Father and the Spirit concur'd to it, yet the Redeeming work was peculiarly terminated in the second person. The other two persons have a right of propriety to Redeem us. Christ onely a right of propin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quity as assuming our nature, and being of Kin to us.</ns0:note> we <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">We elect before mentioned.</ns0:note> have redemption <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Freedom from the Wrath of God, and Curse of the Law to which we are obnoxious, and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sequently the Power of Sin and Tyranny of Satan, as the ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fects of the former.</ns0:note> through his bloud <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> By the Sacrifice of his Death upon the Cross where his Bloud was shed. This was the price of Redemption paid to God for us, and wherewith his justice being satisfied, we could no longer be detained under the custody of the Devil, or the dominion of Sin.</ns0:note>, even the forgiveness of sins <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Redemp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion is not Formally forgiveness, but Casually, forgiveness being the effect of it; and it is mentioned not as the onely or adequate, but the prime and principal fruit of Redemp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and upon which the other depend.</ns0:note>, accor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ding to the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chap. 3.8, 16. Phil. 4.19.</ns0:note> riches of his grace <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">What he called Glorious Grace, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. here he calls Riches of Grace, meaning plentifull and superabundant Grace, by a Phrase frequently used by him elsewhere in the same sense, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.23. <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2.4, 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Wherein he hath abounded <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">In which Grace before mentioned he hath abounded to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward us; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> out of abundance of Grace in himself (called Rich<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es of Grace, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.) he hath bestowed upon us wisedom and prudence. The like expression we have, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.14.</ns0:note> toward us in all <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This denotes either, the perfections or excellency of it, being in stead of all other wisedom, and more excellent than all else, or <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> in comparison of what was under the Old Testament. They then had Divine Truths revealed but by parts and parcels, and so a more sparing measure of spiritual wise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, but under the Gospel, Believers have it more fully and largely, the Spirit of Wisedom, and Revelation being poured out on them.</ns0:note> wisedom and prudence <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either the Doctrine of the Gospel which contains more perfect, and higher wisedom than that the <ns0:hi>Greeks</ns0:hi> sought after, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.22. and for lack of which, they counted the Gospel Foolishness; or rather, by <ns0:hi>Wisedom</ns0:hi> is understood that Knowledge or Faith whereby we receive Spiritual Truths revealed to us, and to be believed by us, so as to their excellency, and have our hearts affected with them; and by <ns0:hi>Prudence</ns0:hi> the Knowledge of the rule of our Duty with skill to govern our selves according to it: And so Wisedom is no other than Faith, and Prudence the same in effect with Holiness; the former relates to the things we are to Believe, the latter to the things we are to Doe. In the working these two in the Soul, consists inward and effectual calling, which the Apostle mentions in this Verse as he doth the outward likewise, by the Preaching the Word of the Gospel in the next.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16.25. Col. 1.26.</ns0:note> Having made known <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Having revealed to us outwardly by the Preaching of the Gospel; inwardly by the Illumination of the Spirit.</ns0:note> unto us the mys<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tery of his will <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The whole Doctrine of Grace and Salvation by Christ, which is a secret to others, and had still been so to us, had not God discovered it to us in the Gospel.</ns0:note> according to his good plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The good pleasure of God, is the fountain of all spiritual Blessings which flow out to us, aswell as it is of our being first chosen and appointed to be the Subjects of them.</ns0:note> which he hath purposed in himself <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This signifies a firm setled will in God, either meerly of God, and moved by nothing out of himself, or his keeping this purpose in himself till the time appointed for the publication of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 That in the dispensation <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">In that admi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistration or distribution of the good things of God s house, which he had determined should be in the fulness of time. It is a Metaphor taken from a Steward who distributes and dispenseth according to his Master's order to those that are in the house, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 12.42. The Church is the House of God, God himself the Master of the Family, Christ the Steward that governs the House; those spiritual Blessings mentioned, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. are the good things he gives out. These Treasures of God's Grace had been opened but to a few, and dispensed sparingly under the Old Testament, the more full communication of them being reserved till the fulness of times when they were to be dispensed by Christ.</ns0:note> of the fulness of times <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The time appointed of the Father for the appearance of Christ in the flesh (according to former promises) the promulgation of the Gospel, and thereby the gathering together in one, all things in Christ: It is spoken in opposition to the times and ages before Christ's coming, which God would have run out till the set time came which he had pitched upon, and Believers expected; see <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.2, 4.</ns0:note>, he might gather together in one <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To <ns0:hi>recapitulate</ns0:hi>; either to sum up, as men do several lesser numbers in one total sum, which is the foot of the account, but called by the <ns0:hi>Greeks</ns0:hi> the head of it, and set at the top; or as Orators do the several parts of their Speeches in fewer words; thus all former prophecies, promises, types and shadows center'd, and were fulfilled, and as it were summed up in Christ: or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, to unite unto, and gather together again under one head things before divided, and scattered.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 1.2</ns0:note> all things <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">All intellectual beings, or all persons, as <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.22.</ns0:note> in Christ <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As their head under which they might be united to God, and to each other.</ns0:note>, both which are in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>the H<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>vens.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either Saints departed, who have already obtained Sal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation by Christ, or rather the Holy Angels that still keep their first station.</ns0:note>, and which are on earth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Elect of God among men here upon earth in their several Generations. The meaning of the whole seems to be, that whereas the order and harmony of God's principal Workmanship, Intellectual Creatures, Angels and Men had been disturbed and broken by the en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tring of Sin into the World; all Mankind, and many of the Angels having Apostatiz'd from him, and the remnant of them being in their own nature labile and mutable; God would in his appointed time, give Christ (the Heir of all things) the Honour of being the repairer of this Breach, by gathering together again the disjointed members of his Creation in and under Christ as their Head and Governour, confirming the good Angels in their good estate, and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />covering his Elect among men from their Apostate condi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion. Though it be true, that not onely Believers under the Old Testament were saved, but the Elect Angels con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmed before Christ's coming, yet both the one and the o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther was with a respect to Christ as their Head, and the foundation of their Union with God, and out of whom, as the one being lost could not have been restored, so the fall of the other could not have been prevented, nor their hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piness secured.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> in him.<ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Some Copies join the last clause of the former Verse with this, leaving out the relative <ns0:hi>which,</ns0:hi> and concluding the sentence at <ns0:hi>good pleasure,</ns0:hi> and then reade <ns0:hi>He purposed in himself that in the dispensation,</ns0:hi> &c. but most reade it as our Translators have rendred it, onely some understand an explicative particle <ns0:hi>to wit</ns0:hi> in the beginning of this Verse, <ns0:hi>To wit, that in the dispensation,</ns0:hi> &c. but either way the scope of the words is the same, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to give the sum of that <ns0:hi>mystery</ns0:hi> of God's <ns0:hi>will</ns0:hi> mentioned before.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 In whom we <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">We Apostles and others Elect of the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Nation, we <ns0:hi>who first trusted in Christ,</ns0:hi> v. 12.</ns0:note> also have obtained an in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Are called, or brought into the participation of an Inheritance, or have a Right given us to it as by lot. In allusion to the twelve Tribes, having in the Division of the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> their Inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritances assigned them by lot. He shews that they did not first seek it, much less deserve it, but God cast it upon them: their lot fell in the Heavenly Inheritance when others did not.</ns0:note>, being predestinated <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This, aswell as the forementioned privileges, was designed to us by eternal Predestination, and though it be free, and without our procuring, yet in respect of God, it is not casual, but of his ordering.</ns0:note> according to the purpose of him who worketh <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Powerfully and effectually;</ns0:note> all things af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter the councel of his own will <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That infinite wisedom of God which is always in con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />junction with his will, whereby he acts wisely aswell as freely, and though not by deliberation which falls beneath his infi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nite perfection, yet with his greatest reason and judgment.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:485" />12 That we should be to the praise of his glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either 1. Passively, that the excellency and greatness of God's Wisedom, Power, Grace, Mercy, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> might be shewn forth in us by our being predestinated, called, sanc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tified, saved: or 2. rather Actively, that we by the holiness, obedience, and fruitfulness of our conversations suitable to such privileges, might manifest and set forth the Glory of him that vouchsafed them to us.</ns0:note> who first <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>hoped.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> trusted in Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who were the fruits of the New Testament Church, the Gospel having been first Preached to the Apostles by Christ himself, and by them to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> (their own Nation) and having been first believed by them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 In whom ye <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Ye <ns0:hi>Ephesians</ns0:hi> and other <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> also <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">Here is a defect of the Verb in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> which may be supplied either from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. which seems to be the prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipal Verb in the sentence, and then it must be read, <ns0:hi>In whom ye also have obtained an Inheritance:</ns0:hi> or from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12. <ns0:hi>trusted,</ns0:hi> which is the nearest Verb, so our Translation, <ns0:hi>In whom ye also trusted,</ns0:hi> but neither way makes any difference in the scope of the words.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>trusted</ns0:hi> after ye heard the word of truth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Gospel, so called either by an usual <ns0:hi>Hebraism</ns0:hi> from the true word, or by way of Eminency, as containing the most excellent and necessary of all Truths, the Doctrine of Righteousness and Life by Jesus Christ; or 3. with respect to the Law and its shadows, the truth and substance of which, is held forth in the Gospel,</ns0:note> the gospel of your salva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">both in respect of the matter contained in it, the Doctrine of Salvation, and in respect of its efficiency, as being the means whereby God works Faith, and brings to Salvation, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.12. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 2.3.</ns0:note>; in whom <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>In whom</ns0:hi> either is to be referred to Believers: <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> after ye believed in Christ, or to Sealing, and then it shews by virtue of whom this benefit of Sealing is bestowed, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> by virtue of Christ.</ns0:note> also after that ye believed, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Cor. 1.22.</ns0:note> ye were sealed with that holy spirit <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Ye were secured and ascertained of your Right to the Inheritance; which we may understand to be done either by the Spirit's impressing upon the Soul, the Image of God in the Work of Regeneration, or be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause that cannot so well be understood to be after believing) rather by his Testinomy in mens own Consciences afterward, whether immediate by an overpowring light, shining into the Soul, and filling it with assurance of its Interest in Christ and Heaven, or mediate, enabling a man to discern that Image of God in his Soul, by which the Spirit bears Witness to his interest in the Inheritance, and assures him of it; see <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.30. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.16. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.6.</ns0:note> of pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Because the Spirit's coming was before promised, or because he verifies and confirms the Promises, in and to the Hearts of Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lievers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 5.5.</ns0:note> Which is the earnest of our inheritance <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Spirit given to, and dwelling in Believers by his Gifts and Graces is the earnest or pledge whereby their In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance is secured to them, as Men are secured the pay<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of a promised Sum, by a part given beforehand in earnest for the rest.</ns0:note> until the redemption of the purchased possession <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either 1. the Redemption of the Possession is put for the Possessing of the Redemption (by an Hypallage) <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> full and final Redemption from Sin, and Death, and Hell, and Satan; which Redemption though perfectly wrought by Christ, is but in part applied in this Life, and is to be fully enjoyed in the other; or 2. rather (though to the same sense) to the full and final Redemption in the end of the World, of all God's people who are here called his Purchased Possession: see the same word so ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken, <ns0:hi>Act</ns0:hi> 20.28. and 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.9.</ns0:note>, unto the praise of his glory <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The final Salvation, and complete Redemption of God's people, will be espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially for the Glory of God, 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Wherefore I also, <ns0:note place="margin">Co<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 1.4.</ns0:note> after I heard <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He was an Eye Witness of their first believing, but here he speaks of their encrease and constancy in the Faith since, of which he had heard by others:</ns0:note> of your faith in the Lord Jesus <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> not barely a Belief of Christ's Excellencies, but a belief of his being their Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour, their receiving and relying on him as such, and so a Believing in him as the immediate object of their Faith, and him by whom they believed in God, 1. <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.21.</ns0:note>, and love to all the saints <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This is added to shew the Truth of their Faith which works by love. Love to the Saints is mentioned as an Evidence of their Love to God, and to <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> the Saints, to shew the sincerity of that Love in its not being partial, but respecting all Saints, and therefore Saints as Saints.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Rom. 1.9. Phil. 1.3<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 4. 1 Thess. 1.2. 2 Thess. 1.3.</ns0:note> Cease not to give thanks for you <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For your Faith and Love, and all the spiritual Blessings God hath bestowed upon you.</ns0:note> ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king mention of you in my prayers <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I not onely acknowledge what ye have received, but pray that what is yet lacking in you may be made up.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 That <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 20.17.</ns0:note> the God of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He is the God of Christ not according to Christ's Divine Nature, but his Humane, and as Mediatour, in which respect he was subject to the Father.</ns0:note>, the Father of glory <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The most glorious Father, and the Authour of all Glory, and glorious things, and to whom all glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry is due.</ns0:note> may give unto you the spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of wisedom <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">A greater measure (for some they already had) of Faith (as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. where it is called Wisedom) or of the knowledge of the things of God, whereof the Spirit is the Authour, God is said to give or send the Spirit, where the Spirit works effectually, and so to give the Spirit of Wise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, where the Spirit effectually works that Wisedom.</ns0:note>, and revelation <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By Revelation he means not extraordinary, such as the Prophets had, but ordinary, such as was common to Belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers, and expresseth the manner of the Spirit's working this wisedom, that he doth it by removing the covering or veil of natural Ignorance, (<ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119.18. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 24.45.) shining into the mind, and making it see what before it saw not; sometimes new objects, sometimes new excellencies in ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects before known. Thus the Spirit works not onely in the beginning of Faith and spiritual Knowledge, but in its farther progress he lets in new Light into the mind, and removes some remaining degree of natural Darkness.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>for the acknowledge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in the know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>Acknowledgement,</ns0:hi> which may imply an owning, approving, and embracing things before known.</ns0:note> of him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God or Christ, or God in Christ: and so either he declares here wherein the Wisedom he mentioned consists, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the Knowledge of God and Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of Wise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom and Knowledge: or rather the end of that Wisedom and Revelation, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the acknowledgement of God or Christ, when we so know him, as to own him as ours, to embrace, and love, and wholly subject our selves to him, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.9, 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 The eyes of your understanding being en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lightned <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Viz.</ns0:hi> By that Spirit of Revelation: and so this clause explains the former. What the Eye is to the Body, that the Understanding is to the Soul. He prays for a farther degree of Illumination for them.</ns0:note>, that ye may know what is the hope of his calling <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either 1. the object of Hope, the thing hoped for, as <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.5. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.5. and then the meaning is, What it is to the Hope of which God hath called you by the Gospel. Or 2. the Grace of Hope, <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> that ye may know how great, and sure, and well grounded that hope is, which by the Gospel is wrought in you.</ns0:note>, and what the riches of the glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The glorious riches, or the abundant glory; Riches of Glory, and Riches of Grace, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. and Riches of Glory, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9.23.</ns0:note> of his <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">because he is the Father of it: he gives this Glory as the Father of Glory. As Men give Inheritances suitable to their Estates, so God as the God of Glory, and Father of Glory, gives a Glorious Inheritance.</ns0:note> inheritance <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heaven, called an Inheritance both in respect of Believers Title to it by virtue of their Adoption being Heirs of God, and in respect of the per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />petuity of their enjoying it, on which account it is called an E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal Inheritance, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.15.</ns0:note> in the Saints <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">or <ns0:hi>among</ns0:hi> the Saints, those namely that are perfect, who alone are possessed of the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />heritance, which Saints on earth have onely in hope.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He means that Power of God which is put forth in the whole of our Salvation, from first to last: not that absolute power whereby he can doe whatsoever is possible to be done, but his ordinate power, or power joined with his will, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by not onely he will work in raising us up at last, and finally saving us, but hath wrought in begetting Faith in us, and doth work in still preserving that Faith (1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.5.) and carry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing us on in the way of Salvation. And this he speaks for the en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />couragement of the <ns0:hi>Ephesians,</ns0:hi> that they should not fea<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> falling short of the Riches of the Glory of the Inheritance mentioned, seeing God who hath by his power brought them to Christ, is able likewise by the same power to bring them to Glory.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 2.12.</ns0:note> according to the working <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Of the might of his power.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> of his mighty power <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Some point the words after <ns0:hi>us-ward,</ns0:hi> and reade them, <ns0:hi>Who believe according to the working of his mighty power,</ns0:hi> &c. and then the meaning must be, that the working Faith in Believers, is an instance of his mighty power: he hath shewn his power in working Faith, and therefore will shew it in the remainder of Salvation which is to follow. But our Translation favours the former sense, and then as in the preceding Clause he shews the greatness of God's Power, so in this latter the Efficacy of it in its actual Ope<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration, particularly the raising up Christ from the Dead.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">

                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The PowerGod exerciseth toward Believers is such as that was whereby he raised up Christ from the Dead.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 110.1.</ns0:note> set him at his own right hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Hath invested him with the greatest Honour, Dignity, and Power, as Princes set the next in honour, and authority to themselves at their Right Hands: see <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 20.21.</ns0:note> in the heavenly <ns0:hi>places</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">In the highest Heaven, called the third Heaven, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12.2. and Paradise, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 2.5. Col. 2.10.</ns0:note> Far above all principality and power, and might, and dominion <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">These terms are sometimes applied to Magistrates, and Men in Authority here in the World, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 3.1. <ns0:hi>Iude</ns0:hi> 8. sometimes to Angels, Good Ones, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.16. to Evil Ones, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.12. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.15. though with allusion to Powers in the World, or because by them God puts forth and ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />

                     </ns0:gap>ciseth his Power and Dominion. By these then the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle understands good Angels, as <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3.10. or compre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hensively, all sorts of Powers both visible and invisible, as <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.16. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.22.</ns0:note>, and every name that is named <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest any might think he had not named all above whom Christ is exalted, he adds this, to take all in. Every <ns0:hi>name,</ns0:hi> that is, every Person, and every thing which hath a Name: whatever hath any Dignity or Excellency.</ns0:note> not onely in this World, but also in that which is to come <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Because though it hath a being at present, yet it is future to us who are not yet possessed of it. Either this Clause relates to Christ's Sitting at his Father's Right Hand, and then it notes the perpetuity of his Reign, that his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom is an everlasting Kingdom, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 1.33. or rather to the words immediately going before: <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> if there be any Name, any Dignity or Excellency not known in this Life, and which shall be known in the other; yet be they what they may, Christ is above them all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

They are begun to be subjected to him, and by degrees shall be farther subjected till they be perfectly and absolutely subjected unto him, <ns0:hi>de facto</ns0:hi> as al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready they are <ns0:hi>de jure,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> and gave him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">appointed or constituted or made him.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> head <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A mystical Head: such a one not onely as a King is to his Subjects to Rule them externally by his Laws, but such as a natural Head is to the Body, which it governs by way of Influence, conveying Spirits to it, and so causing and maintaining sense and motion in it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.16. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.19.</ns0:note> over all things <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either 1. God hath chiefly, and above all before mentioned, given Christ to be the Head of the Church; <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> though he be King and Lord of all, yet God hath made him the onely proper Head to the Church onely; God hath set him above Principalities and Powers, but especially hath appointed him to be the Head of the Church. Or 2. over all things may be meant for the Communication of all good things to the Church, and performing all Offices of an Head to her: an Head to the Church with a Power over all things for her good.</ns0:note> to the Churches <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Catholick Church, or whole Col<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lection of Believers throughout the World, and in all A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 12.27. ch. 4.12. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 5.23, 30. Col. 1.18.</ns0:note> Which is his body <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A mystical one, whereof every Member is influ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />enced by the Spirit of Christ the Head, as in the natural Body the Members are influenced by Spirits derived from the natural Head.</ns0:note>, the fulness of him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The Church is called the Fulness of Christ not Personally but Relatively considered, and as Head of the Church: The Head is incomplete without the Body; Christ in his Relative capacity as a Head would not be complete without his mystical Body the Church.</ns0:note>
